content: An API oil-water separator is a specialized device engineered to separate significant quantities of oil and suspended solids from wastewater effluents originating from oil refineries, petrochemical plants, chemical plants, natural gas processing facilities, and other industrial sources. The term API is derived from the fact that these separators are designed in accordance with standards established by the American Petroleum Institute (API). The API separator operates as a gravity-based separation system, utilizing Stokes' Law to calculate the rise velocity of oil droplets based on their density and size. The design is predicated on the specific gravity difference between oil and wastewater, which is smaller than the specific gravity difference between suspended solids and water. Consequently, suspended solids settle at the bottom of the separator, forming a sediment layer, while oil rises to the top, and the wastewater occupies the middle layer between the oil and the solids. In practice, the oil layer is skimmed off for reprocessing or disposal, while the sediment layer at the bottom is removed using a chain-and-flight scraper or a similar mechanism, along with a sludge pump. The middle water layer is directed to further treatment, typically involving a dissolved air flotation (DAF) unit to remove residual oil, followed by a biological treatment unit to eliminate undesirable dissolved chemical compounds. Parallel plate separators function similarly to API separators but incorporate tilted parallel plate assemblies, also known as parallel packs. The underside of each plate provides additional surface area for suspended oil droplets to coalesce into larger globules, while sediment slides down the topside of the plates. These separators still rely on the specific gravity difference between oil and water but achieve enhanced oil-water separation due to the parallel plates. As a result, parallel plate separators require significantly less space than conventional API separators to achieve comparable separation efficiency. The API separator was first developed approximately 75 years ago by the American Petroleum Institute in collaboration with the Rex Chain Belt Company. The inaugural API separator was installed in 1933 at the Atlantic Refining Company (ARCO) refinery in Philadelphia. Since then, nearly all refineries worldwide have incorporated API separators into their wastewater treatment systems. While many refineries initially adopted the original design based on the specific gravity difference between oil and water, numerous facilities now utilize plastic parallel plate packing to improve gravity separation performance. Beyond industrial wastewater treatment, oil-water separation has other critical applications. For instance, oily water separators (OWS) are employed to separate oil from bilge water in ships, as mandated by the international MARPOL Convention. Additionally, oil-water separators are commonly used in electrical substations, where transformers rely on large volumes of oil for cooling. Surrounding moats are constructed to capture leaked oil, but they also collect rainwater. In such cases, oil-water separators facilitate quicker and more efficient cleanup of oil leaks.
